passage: Sun, 9:40 pm. Tanuja has looked blank for three weeks. At the stand-up she stares at the wall, answers in one word, no smile. I nearly told my manager she seems checked out. Then today I saw her in the pantry, holding a cup of tea and not drinking it, just standing. She looked so tired. I said, "Want to walk to the gate for some air?" and she came. She said the release plus her father's hospital visits has left her flat. I offered to take over the test report for a week. She teared up a little and thanked me. I am glad I did not judge her attitude. I am Nikita, by the way, and I feel a bit guilty for the thoughts I had earlier. 🙂

qa.a: She probably felt relieved and slightly emotional to be noticed kindly, since she teared up when she got practical help.

subtype: Blank expression in exhaustion or burnout [Interpreting]
passage: At the milk cooperative in the kasba, Vishal had stopped joking with the farmers weeks ago. He logged the fat readings with a face like a wall: no smile when little Munni brought her family's can, no reply when the supervisor praised his accounts. Jagdish heard two loaders mutter that Vishal thought he was too good for the job now. Jagdish wasn't sure. The blankness looked more tired than proud; there were grey shadows under his eyes, and twice his tiffin had gone home unopened. That evening, after the last tanker left, Jagdish sat beside him on the loading step. "You've looked worn out for a while. Anything going on?" Vishal stared at the road. "My mother's in the district hospital. I sleep there." Jagdish nodded slowly. "I'll take the morning collection this week. Go and sleep."

qa.q: Where does Vishal sleep at night?
qa.a: In the district hospital, where his mother is.

qa.q: What did Jagdish think Vishal's blank face might mean?
qa.a: Jagdish felt uneasy and concerned, sensing the blankness looked more tired than proud because of the shadows and unopened tiffin, though it could also have been a mood with another cause.

qa.q: What made Jagdish's response helpful?
qa.a: Jagdish checked in privately after work, named the tiredness kindly without judging, and then offered practical help by taking the morning collection.

qa.q: How might the loaders have seen Vishal differently if they knew about the hospital?
qa.a: They might feel sorry and sympathetic instead of resentful, reading his blank face as exhaustion rather than pride.

grounding: Shows a colleague's weeks-long blank face read as exhaustion rather than disinterest, followed by a private check-in and practical help.

passage: In the Lisbon design studio, Xin had gone quiet in a way people noticed. For three weeks at the Monday stand-up her face stayed flat, eyes on the table, no reaction even when the director announced the new museum contract. "She's checked out," someone whispered to Priscila afterwards. Priscila had worked beside Xin for two years and remembered her laughing at stand-ups until her eyes watered. This stillness looked heavier than boredom. On Wednesday she caught Xin at the coffee machine, away from the others. "You seem really drained lately. You don't have to explain, but I'm around." Xin rubbed her eyes. "Since Marta left I've been doing both our client lists. I finish at midnight." Priscila picked up her mug. "Give me the hotel account. And let's ask the director about Marta's list together tomorrow."

qa.q: How long had Xin's face stayed flat at stand-ups?
qa.a: For three weeks.

qa.a: Priscila felt concerned rather than annoyed, because she remembered Xin laughing at stand-ups and the stillness looked heavier than boredom; disinterest was possible, but it didn't fit Xin.

qa.q: What practical help did Priscila offer, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She took the hotel account and offered to raise Marta's list with the director together, easing Xin's load instead of only sympathising.

qa.q: What might it be like for Xin when colleagues read her face as boredom?
qa.a: Xin may feel unseen and more alone, working until midnight while people think she doesn't care.

grounding: Shows a colleague reading weeks of blank expression as overload rather than disinterest and responding with a private check-in and practical help.

subtype: Blank expression in exhaustion or burnout [Interpreting]
passage: In the staffroom of the girls' senior secondary school, Bhavna had become someone the others talked about. For almost a month she had graded copies with a face that didn't move, not even when the Class 9 kids brought her a birthday card. "Attitude," the vice-principal muttered at the tea urn. Jasleen, who taught in the next room, wasn't convinced. Bhavna's blankness came with a slow, heavy way of standing up, and she was the first to arrive and the last to leave. After the last bell Jasleen walked with her to the bus stop, just the two of them. "You don't have to be cheerful for me," she said. "Are you managing?" Bhavna let out a long breath. "Exam duty, the new timetable, and my baby's teething. I haven't slept properly in weeks." Jasleen said, "Give me your Saturday invigilation. I'm free."

qa.q: What did the Class 9 kids bring Bhavna?
qa.a: A birthday card.

qa.q: What did Jasleen think Bhavna's still face might mean, and why?
qa.a: Jasleen felt worried and doubtful about the 'attitude' label, since the blankness came with heavy movements and long hours, suggesting exhaustion rather than rudeness.

qa.q: How did Jasleen's check-in avoid making things worse?
qa.a: She spoke privately on the walk, told Bhavna she didn't need to act cheerful, and offered concrete help by taking the Saturday invigilation.

qa.q: How might the vice-principal's view change after hearing about Bhavna's weeks?
qa.a: The vice-principal might feel sorry for judging and see the blank face as tiredness, perhaps easing the load instead of criticising.

grounding: Shows a colleague's weeks-long blank face understood as exhaustion through a private, kind check-in and an offer of practical help.

Hi Charu,
I wanted to write rather than catch you in the corridor, because this isn't about the quality of your work.
For the past few weeks I've noticed you look very still in our stand-ups, no reaction even when someone told that terrible pun about the printer. I'll admit that at first I wondered if you'd lost interest in the project. Then I remembered you stayed till nine twice last week and never said a word about it.
So I'm not assuming anything. You might be tired, or a lot might be going on, or I might be reading too much into a face. If you're carrying too much, I can move the vendor reports to another teammate for a month, and you can skip Friday's call.
Would you like to grab coffee on Thursday, just us? No agenda.
Take care,
Uma

qa.a: Uma offers to move the vendor reports to another teammate for a month.

qa.a: Uma was first worried that Charu had lost interest in the project, but felt less sure after remembering that Charu stayed till nine twice last week.

qa.a: It is private, says it isn't about work quality, avoids assuming, and offers practical help plus an unhurried coffee.

qa.a: Charu might feel relieved and seen, since the email offers help without judging; Charu could also feel a bit exposed that the blank face was noticed.
